Georges Méliès. A French pioneering filmmaker and illusionist who invented trick cinematography and the language of special effects, transforming cinema from a mechanical novelty into a vehicle for fantasy and imagination. His A Trip to the Moon is cinema's first science-fiction film and a foundational text in film history, establishing the syntax of the fantastical narrative film.

He created A Trip to the Moon in 1902, a fourteen-minute film depicting a group of astronomers launching a spacecraft to the moon, encountering aliens, and returning—a prototype for science fiction. Méliès pioneered stop-motion photography, replacing actors and scenery by stopping the camera to substitute elements, inventing the fundamental grammar of special effects. He used theatrical staging and painted backdrops transferred from his magic shows. For him, cinema was an extension of theatrical illusion, not a capturing of reality.

He directed over five hundred films between 1896 and 1914, establishing narrative cinema long before Griffith's innovations. His films circulated worldwide, making him among the first international film stars and establishing the commercial viability of cinema as entertainment. However, Méliès suffered financial ruin during World War I. His films were lost or destroyed for decades, and he worked as a magician and toy seller before his rediscovery in the nineteen-thirties.

He remains foundational to cinema history—the originator of narrative cinema and the artist who showed cinema's magical potential. The Lumière brothers were his contemporaries pioneering cinema, but while they documented, Méliès commercialised. He established the genre of science fiction cinema and its visual language. Later narrative pioneers like David Wark Griffith built on the foundations Méliès established. He invented the fundamental technique of special effects.
